Mithredath
MITH-reh-dath
n. (proper name; Cyrus's treasurer, and a Persian official of Artaxerxes' reign)
Persian, meaning given by Mithras — a theophoric name formed on the Persian deity Mithra. The Greek form of the same name is Mithridates.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Mithredath is named twice, of two Persian officials. The first is the man who handed back the temple vessels: “Even those did Cyrus king of Persia bring forth by the hand of Mithredath the treasurer, and numbered them unto Sheshbazzar, the prince of Judah” (Ezra 1:8). Nebuchadnezzar had carried the vessels of the house of the LORD into the house of his gods (Ezra 1:7); seventy years later a Persian treasurer counted them out again, five thousand four hundred pieces of gold and silver, into the hands of a prince of Judah (Ezra 1:11). The second Mithredath writes to Artaxerxes to stop the rebuilding (Ezra 4:7). The Authorized Version prints the name twice. The dictionary notes what the first verse demonstrates. God used a pagan emperor, named by Isaiah a hundred and fifty years before he was born, and a treasurer named after a Persian god, to restore the vessels of His own worship. Providence does not require its instruments to be believers. The vessels went out under judgment and came back by inventory, counted by a man whose name honoured Mithras.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) gives no entry for Mithredath; the name is Persian and belongs to Cyrus's treasurer and to a later official under Artaxerxes.

Webster (1828) gives no entry for Mithredath.

The name appears at Ezra 1:8 and Ezra 4:7.

It is Persian, meaning given by Mithras; the Greek form is Mithridates.

The first bearer is the treasurer who delivered the temple vessels to Sheshbazzar.

The second writes to Artaxerxes against the rebuilding of Jerusalem.

Key Scripture

Ezr 1:8 — "Even those did Cyrus king of Persia bring forth by the hand of Mithredath the treasurer, and numbered them unto Sheshbazzar, the prince of Judah."

Ezr 1:7 — "Also Cyrus the king brought forth the vessels of the house of the LORD, which Nebuchadnezzar had brought forth out of Jerusalem, and had put them in the house of his gods;"

Ezr 1:11 — "All the vessels of gold and of silver were five thousand and four hundred. All these did Sheshbazzar bring up with them of the captivity that were brought up from Babylon unto Jerusalem."

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.

expand to see more

The return under Cyrus is routinely explained as ordinary Persian imperial policy toward subject religions, which it also was. That explanation is not wrong; it is incomplete. Isaiah had named Cyrus by name and called him the LORD's shepherd and His anointed long before, and Ezra 1:1 says the LORD stirred up his spirit. Secondary causes are real and are not the first cause.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the freedom of providence in its instruments. A treasurer named for Mithras counted out the vessels of the house of the LORD and handed them to a prince of Judah, and God was served by every hand in the transaction.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Persian Mithredath, given by Mithras; the treasurer who delivered the temple vessels to Sheshbazzar at Ezra 1:8.

expand to see more

Persian, formed on the god Mithra: given by Mithras.

The Greek form of the same name is Mithridates.

Ezra 1:8 and Ezra 4:7 are the two occurrences.

Five thousand four hundred vessels of gold and silver were returned.

Nebuchadnezzar had placed them in the house of his gods.

Usage

"by the hand of Mithredath the treasurer"

"numbered them unto Sheshbazzar, the prince of Judah"

"five thousand and four hundred"
